intro.html: This topic is the mirror image of Making Things Better. Some of these verbs describe making a bad situation worse (exacerbate, aggravate, compound); some describe slow weakening, often from below or out of sight (undermine, erode, deteriorate); and some describe damage or danger (debilitate, impair, jeopardize, sabotage).

Make a bad thing worse: exacerbate, aggravate, compound. Weaken slowly: undermine (from beneath, or in secret), erode (wear away), deteriorate (grow worse). Damage and danger: debilitate (weaken badly), impair (damage), jeopardize (put at risk), sabotage (wreck on purpose).

words.def: to make a problem or pain worse
words.ex: Scratching a mosquito bite only {exacerbates} the itch.
words.ctx: The drought was bad enough, but the town {exacerbated} the problem by watering its golf course every afternoon while the reservoir dried up.
words.etym: From Latin exacerbare, “to irritate, to make harsh”: ex (thoroughly) + acerbus (harsh, bitter).

mn.cue: ex-ACERB-ate: add more SOUR to the sour
mn.text: Kai is already puckering from one lemon, and his brother hands him another. Adding sour to sour is how you {exacerbate} a problem.

scene.alt: A boy makes a sour face from a lemon while his brother offers another.

words.def: to make worse; also, in everyday speech, to annoy
words.ex: Lifting heavy boxes {aggravated} the coach’s sore back.
words.ctx: Instead of calming the argument, Pip {aggravated} it by reminding his sister of every unfair thing she had ever done.
words.etym: From Latin aggravare, “to make heavier”: ad (to) + gravis (heavy).
words.note: Careful writers use aggravate to mean make worse; the sense “annoy” is common in everyday speech.

mn.text: Sami’s backpack is already heavy, and then Jonah sneaks a big rock into it. Grav means heavy: to {aggravate} a problem is to make it heavier.

scene.alt: A sneaky teen slips a rock into a hiker’s already heavy backpack.

words.ex: Constant teasing can {undermine} a child’s confidence.
words.ctx: Though he praised the plan in public, the manager quietly {undermined} it, canceling its meetings and moving its money to other projects.
words.etym: From under + mine: to dig a tunnel beneath a wall so that it collapses.

mn.text: A rabbit tunnels under the sandcastle’s tallest tower, and day by day the tower leans a little more. Weakening something from underneath is to {undermine} it.

scene.alt: A rabbit digs under a sandcastle, which begins to lean, while a girl gasps.

words.ex: Waves {eroded} the cliff a little more each winter.
words.ctx: Small broken promises {eroded} the team’s trust in its captain: no single one mattered much, but together they wore it away.
words.etym: From Latin erodere, “to gnaw away”: e (away) + rodere (to gnaw), the root of rodent.

mn.cue: e-RODE: gnawed away, as by a RODent
mn.text: Night after night, a little mouse nibbles the big wheel of cheese until only a sliver is left. Rodere means to gnaw: water, wind and time {erode} things the same slow way.

labels.text: e-RODE: gnawed away, bit by bit

scene.alt: A mouse nibbles away at a big wedge of cheese on the kitchen table.

words.ex: Left out in the rain, the old book {deteriorated} until its pages stuck together.
words.ctx: The weather {deteriorated} as the hikers climbed: sunshine gave way to clouds, then sleet, and finally a blinding snowstorm.
words.etym: From Latin deteriorare, “to make worse,” from deterior, worse.

mn.text: Kai’s old kite starts with one small tear; after a week of wind, it is more holes than kite. It has {deteriorated}.

scene.alt: A sad boy flies a battered, torn kite in the wind.

words.ex: The long heat wave {debilitated} the garden’s tomato plants.
words.ctx: The flu {debilitated} Sami for a week; he was so weak that a walk to the kitchen left him needing a nap.
words.etym: From Latin debilitare, “to weaken,” from debilis, weak.

mn.text: Day after day of blazing heat drains every bit of strength from the sunflowers until they droop to the ground. A heat wave can {debilitate} a garden.

scene.alt: Under a blazing sun, sunflowers droop to the ground while a girl looks on, worried.

words.ex: Very loud music can {impair} your hearing over time.
words.ctx: Thick fog {impaired} the drivers’ view so badly that the town closed the bridge until it lifted at noon.
words.etym: From Old French empeirier, “to make worse,” based on Latin pejor, worse.

mn.cue: im-PAIR: a smudged PAIR of glasses
mn.text: Grandpa’s pair of glasses is smeared with jam, and now he can barely read the paper. The smudges {impair} his sight.

scene.alt: A grandfather squints at a newspaper through glasses smudged with jam.

words.def: to put in danger or at risk
words.ex: Skipping practice could {jeopardize} Rosa’s spot on the team.
words.ctx: By sharing the secret password with a stranger, Kai {jeopardized} the club’s whole treasure hunt, and the other members had to rewrite every clue.
words.etym: From jeopardy, Old French jeu parti, “a divided game”: a game whose outcome hangs in the balance.

mn.text: Ignoring the THIN ICE sign, Rex skates right out to the middle of the pond, and every crack puts him in jeopardy. He chose to {jeopardize} his own safety.

scene.alt: A man tiptoes on cracking pond ice past a thin-ice sign while a grandmother calls him back.

words.def: to damage or ruin on purpose
words.ex: Someone {sabotaged} the science-fair volcano by swapping the baking soda for flour.
words.ctx: The rival team tried to {sabotage} the race by moving the course markers, but the runners noticed the trick and followed their maps instead.
words.etym: From French saboter, “to botch, to bungle,” from sabot, a wooden shoe.

mn.text: Before the wagon race, Rex creeps over and loosens a wheel on his rival’s wagon. Wrecking something on purpose is to {sabotage} it.

scene.alt: A sneaky man loosens a wheel on a rival’s racing wagon.

words.def: to make a problem worse by adding to it
words.ex: Arriving late, Dev {compounded} the problem by forgetting his uniform.
words.ctx: The town’s mistake in closing the bridge was {compounded} when it closed the ferry too, leaving the island with no way to reach the mainland.
words.etym: From Latin componere, “to put together”: com (together) + ponere (to put).
words.note: Compound also means to combine or mix (to compound a medicine), and interest that compounds grows on itself. As a noun, a compound is a mixture or a fenced group of buildings.

mn.cue: com-POUND: POUND more trouble on top
mn.text: Theo spills his milk, and then the puppy runs through the puddle and tracks white paw prints across the whole house. The puppy {compounded} the problem.

scene.alt: A toddler has spilled his milk, and a puppy runs through it, tracking prints across the floor.

head: how it gets worse
words
rows: weakened from below or in secret

after.html: compound as a verb means to add to a problem (“he compounded the error by lying about it”), not only to combine things. aggravate in careful writing means to make worse; “it really aggravates me” (annoys) is everyday speech.

items.q: The spy made a mistake, then compounded it by lying about it. What did the lie do?
choices: mixed two problems into a cure
items.why: To compound a problem is to make it worse by adding to it.

items.q: Which word best fits weakening something secretly or from beneath?
items.why: Undermine comes from digging a tunnel under a wall; it means to weaken gradually or secretly.

items.q: True or false: erode comes from a Latin word meaning to gnaw, the same root as rodent.
items.why: True. Erode is from Latin erodere, to gnaw away.

items.q: Someone cut the wires to the stadium lights the night before the big game. The game was…
items.why: Damaging something on purpose to make it fail is sabotage.
